docs.text: Neural Networks and Deep Learning Week 1 What is Neural Network Here the neuron takes in the input, x, computes the linear function, takes the max of zero and the x-axis value and outputs the output. This is the simplest neural network and it is called ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit). ReLU = \(f(x) = \max(0, x)\) So we can stack this neurons and create a neural network Supervised Learning with Neural Networks For simple things like price prediction and A/B testing, we use simple standard NN. For Image we use CNN (Convoluted Neural Networks). For sequence data such as Audio and Language we use RNN (Recurrent Neural Networks). And for complex things like autonomous driving we use hybrid models. Neural Networks are really good at handling unstructured data. Such as - Speech Recognition, Image Recognition, Natural Language Processing Why is Deep Learning Taking Off The more data we have, the less performance traditional ML models provide and that is why we are using NN. If we have less amounts of data and a small training set, we do not have any fixed models for that data to train on, it mainly depends on the skill of the engineer on how he handles the different features and data to train the model. But for large amounts of data, generally there are fixed models that will deliver the best performance. The algorithmic improvement has also decreased computational time. One of the improvements is shifting from the use of sigmoid function to a ReLU function, because in the sigmoid function the gradient descent algorithm would run much slower. The sigmoid function, \(S(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}}\) Week 2 Binary Classification In the future we will discuss how to go through the entire training set while training the model, without explicitly using for loops. Also we will learn what forward propagation and backward propagation means when we organize our computations for the neural network. Here if an image is 64 pixels * 64 pixels, it will be represented by 64*64 red, green and blue color channel matrices. Now we need to create a input feature set called X, and the dimension of feature will be \(64 \times 64 \times 3 = 12,288\) and it can be represented by \(n_x\) or \(n\) . Here \(x^{(1)}, x^{(2)}, \dots, x^{(m)}\) are input vectors for images, each one of them is a single image. Together they form a compact input vector, X. Logistic Regression Cost Function for Logistic Regression The loss (error) function is for only one training example. Some of us might think that the squared error would be a good approach for calculating the loss function but as it turns out this approach makes the optimization problem non-convex and thus while using the gradient descent algorithm there are multiple local minimas. So we created a loss function like this - So the total cost function for the whole input will be - \(J(w,b) = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} L(\hat{y}, y) = -\frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left[ y^{(i)} \log \hat{y}^{(i)} + (1 - y^{(i)}) \log (1 - \hat{y}^{(i)}) \right]\) Gradient Descent Here the w, b can be multi-dimensional but for illustration purposes, it’s shown as one dimensional. The height of the z axis shows the value of J(w,b). We are considering the example only for w for simplification purposes. So initially, we assign a value to w, which is traditionally 0 but random assignment also works. But as this is a convex function, no matter what we will assign the value of w, eventually it will reach the global minima. Derivatives This video gives us an intuition about derivatives. The derivative is nothing but a slope \(\frac{height}{width}\) at a. The formal definition is that, if we move the value of a by a tiny amount, what would the value of f(a) be? If \(\frac{d f(a)}{da} = 3\) , That means if we change the value of a by a tiny amount the value of f(a) would be 3 times larger than a. In this case, the slope is unchanged whatever the value of a might be, that is because this is a straight line function. More Derivative Examples Here the slope (or the derivative) value is different for each value of a, as the function is a curve function. Computation Graph In neural networks, the computation is organized as a forward propagation that gives us the final value, J and a backward propagation that gives us the derivatives with respect to J. We will use a computation graph to find out why this is the case and how the values are calculated. Derivatives with a Computation Graph In this slide we are discussing the backward propagation steps and how the different variable slopes are found out with respect to z. Logistic Regression Gradient Descent Here we are finding the values of w1, w2 and b for the logistic regression algorithm using the backpropagation and computation graph. And then we are applying gradient descent on the values - w1, w2 and b. But this example is only for one training example. Logistic Regression on M examples Here we can see the formula of the cost function for \(\frac{d}{d w_1}\) . So what we just have to do is calculate all the \(dw_1(i)\) values. Here after completing the steps for the whole training set, we can apply gradient descent. We can see that there are two loops here, one is to traverse the m training examples, other is to update the various w values from w1 to wn for n number of features. Now using explicit for loops Deep learning models can slow down the model, so we should avoid using for loops and we will learn a new technique called “Vectorization” to do this. Vectorization Vectorization is the technique where we can avoid the explicit use of for-loops that make our model slow. We can calculate for all of the training examples by using just one line, Z \= np.dot(w.T,X) + b, where b \= [b1,b2…bm] More Vectorization Examples Here it shows how to do exponential operations using just one line. Here it shows how to use numpy and eliminate one of the loops that were required to do the backpropagation steps in logistic regression with m examples. Vectorizing Logistic Regression Vectorizing Logistic Regression’s Gradient Output In this example, we saw how we can implement logistic regression, both forward and backward propagation without using any for loops. Week 3 What is a Neural Network In logistic regression, for the forward propagation, we first calculated z using the parameters, then a, then the loss function. For neural networks, we have multiple layers. Each layer can be represented by [i] not to be confused by (i), which indicates the number of training examples. Neural Network Representation This is the architecture of a 2 layer NN. The middle layer is called the hidden layer because we do not have any information about the calculation result done in this layer in the training set. The X or the input set can also be represented by \(a^{[0]}\) . Here ‘a’ means activation and it represents the input that is going to be passed on to the subsequent layer and it has 0 superscript because it is the input layer and the input layer is not counted. Here \(a_1^{[1]}\) means that ‘a’ is the first node of the first layer of the neural network. The hidden layer and the output layer have weights assigned to it. So in this case, the hidden layer has \(w^{[1]}\) and \(b^{[1]}\) weights with shapes (4,3); because there are 4 nodes in the layer and 3 features and (4,1); because 4 nodes in the layer and b is the same for everyone so 1. In the case of the output layer we have \(w^{[2]}\) and \(b^{[2]}\) with shapes (1,4) because the results come from the four nodes of the hidden layer and (1,1) for b. Computing a Neural Networks Output Here one thing to notice is the squared bracket [i] indicates the layer and the subscript z1 refers to the number of nodes in the layer. This is the representation for each node in the hidden layer. As you can see there are four nodes in the hidden layer and for each node we have z and a. So it will be a tedious task to do this for a lot of nodes in the layer, so we need to vectorize this. This is how we can vectorize it - Here wi is a column vector containing the parameter information of x1, x2, x3. So we transpose this column vector into a row vector. The shape is (4,3) as there are 4 nodes in the hidden layer and each there are 3 training examples. And then we can multiply this newly constructed W vector with the X vector which has a shape of (3,1) and then we add it with the B vector. So after this we get the newly constructed Z vector. One rule of thumb for vectorizing is that we need to stack the w, x and b for each of the nodes in each layer. And in the end, this is what we get - Here we can see that, with these four equations we can calculate the output of a 2 layer NN. And if we just ignore everything on the left, the calculations going on in the output layer is essentially similar to logistic regression. Vectorizing Across Multiple Examples Here we can see that we m training examples so we have to find out the output a[2] \= y for each of the training example from x[1] to x[m]. We can see this on the left of the screenshot. So essentially, what we did for one training example x[1] we have to do it for all the training examples from i \= 1 to m. And it is shown on the right side of the screenshot. So to vectorize this first we have to convert all of the related variables to vectors such as X, Z and A. For X, we will have an array of x[1] x[2]....x[m] with the shape (nx, m). For Z and A, we will have an array with shape (number of nodes, m). So if we scan from left to right, we will scan through the training examples and from top to bottom we will go through the number of nodes in the hidden layer. Explanation for Vectorized Implementation This is a screenshot of how the vectorized implementation works. Activation Function Sigmoid Function: 11 + e-z, only useful when the output is between 0 and 1. tanh Function: ez - ezez + ez, strictly better than sigmoid and can be used in the hidden layer. But this kind of function slows down the gradient descent so we can use another kind of function. ReLU Function: The rectified linear unit function. It is a \= max(0,z). Here the derivative is 1 for positive and 0 for negative. And this is why it is faster for gradient descent algorithms to find out the weights and biases. Leaky ReLU: Modified but not so popular version of ReLU. It is a \= max(0.01z, z) Why use Non-Linear Activation Functions A linear function is no better than a standard logistic regression. Using a linear function, we won’t find any interesting or non-linear patterns in the dataset. Adding two linear functions will also result in another linear function. So having a linear function in the hidden layer and the sigmoid in the output layer won’t help much. There’s only one case where we can use linear function is where we are trying to solve a regression problem. Derivatives of Activation Function In the backpropagation phase, we need to find out the derivatives of the activation functions. So here are the derivatives of some common activation functions - Gradient Descent for Neural Networks The gradient descent shown here optimizing the parameters w and b are similarly to what we saw at week 2. In the gradient descent stage we backpropagate from our output layer to our hidden layers and we get dw and db. Finally we update our w and b. Random Initialization We cannot initialize w and b by 0, it works for logistic regression but it does not work for neural networks. We can see in the screenshot that if we initialize w[1] and b[1] as a (n[1], n[0]) shape matrix then there will be symmetry between the results, meaning a1[1] \=a2[1] and dz1[1] \= dz2[1] and it can be proven by induction that it will be symmetric even for a large number of training examples. So what is the solution? We can randomly initialize w and b. w[1] \= np.random.randn((n[1], n[0])) 0.01, we used this 0.01 multiplier so that we get smaller random values for w[1] because then it will be easier for the gradient descent to converge. Otherwise if w gets large then z gets large and so z sits on either the large positive or the large negative part of the activation function where the slope is very minimal and thus the gradient descent takes a long time to converge. b does not have this problem so we can write b[1] \= np.zeros((n[1],1)). Week 4 Getting your Matrix Dimensions Right Intuition about Deep Representations Deep learning models at first detect the simpler things and then go for more complex things as the layers increase.
